title: Micah 6:1–8
context: The prophet calls the people to hear the LORD’s case, with the mountains and the foundations of the earth as witnesses, and the LORD asks, “My people, what have I done to you?” recalling the exodus, Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, and the story of Balak and Balaam. A worshiper then asks how to come before God, whether with burnt offerings, rivers of oil, or even a firstborn child, and the prophet answers, “What does the LORD require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” Both traditions read 6:8 as shared ground: the LORD who redeemed his people calls them to justice, mercy, and humble fellowship with him (cf. Deut 10:12; Hos 6:6).

verses.text: Listen now to what the LORD says: “Arise, plead your case before the mountains, and let the hills hear what you have to say.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Listen now to what the LORD says: “Arise, plead your case before the mountains.”” Arminian readers note the courtroom setting.

The prophet summons the people to hear the LORD’s case.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the covenant lawsuit form.

Shared ground: both traditions read the mountains and hills as witnesses to the covenant, a picture of the seriousness of the LORD’s charge.

verses.text: Hear, you mountains, the LORD’s indictment, and you enduring foundations of the earth; for the LORD has a case against his people, and he will contend with Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The prophet says, “for the LORD has a case against his people, and he will contend with Israel.” Arminian readers note that the LORD himself brings the charge.

The “enduring foundations of the earth” are called to listen.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God holding his people accountable to the covenant.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the LORD’s case rests on his faithfulness and their failure.

verses.text: My people, what have I done to you? How have I burdened you? Answer me!
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks, “My people, what have I done to you? How have I burdened you? Answer me!” Arminian readers note the tenderness of “My people” in the midst of a charge.

The LORD invites them to name any wrong he has done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear God’s grief and his righteousness together.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the people have no case against the LORD, and that his question is both a rebuke and an appeal.

verses.text: For I brought you up out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage. I sent before you Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For I brought you up out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage. I sent before you Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.” Arminian readers note that redemption is the basis of the LORD’s appeal.

Miriam is named among the leaders.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see grace preceding the call to obedience.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a reminder that the LORD’s saving acts come first, and that the people’s response is to flow from them.

verses.text: My people, remember now what Balak king of Moab devised, and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him from Shittim to Gilgal, that you may know the righteous acts of the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“My people, remember now what Balak king of Moab devised, and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him.” Arminian readers note the reference to Numbers 22–24.

The journey “from Shittim to Gilgal” recalls the crossing of the Jordan (cf. Josh 3:1).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the LORD turning a curse into blessing for his people.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that remembering these events shows “the righteous acts of the LORD.”

verses.text: How shall I come before the LORD, and bow myself before the exalted God? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old?
verses.arminianNotes:
The worshiper asks, “How shall I come before the LORD, and bow myself before the exalted God?” Arminian readers note that a new voice responds to the LORD’s case.

The question is about how to approach God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear a sincere but mistaken assumption that more offerings will satisfy God.

Shared ground: both traditions read the question as leading toward 6:8, where the answer is given.

verses.text: Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams? With tens of thousands of rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my disobedience? The fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?
verses.arminianNotes:
The worshiper asks, “Shall I give my firstborn for my disobedience?” Arminian readers note the rising scale of the offers, ending with a firstborn child.

Child sacrifice is condemned elsewhere (cf. 2 Kgs 16:3).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the futility of trying to buy God’s favor.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that no offering, however costly, can substitute for a right relationship with God, and both read the question soberly.

verses.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does the LORD require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
verses.arminianNotes:
“He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does the LORD require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” Arminian readers note that the answer is already known.

Deuteronomy 10:12 asks a similar question.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the life that flows from the LORD’s redemption (6:4).

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a summary of covenant faithfulness, not a rejection of worship, and both connect it with Hosea 6:6 and Matthew 23:23.
